commits.author: rjpower
commits.message:
[finestore] Cut object-store requests per flush and lookup, elect one maintainer, add a simulated S3 backend (#10209)

FineStore writers sharing one archive spent most of their object-store
requests on rename staging, re-reading HEAD before every commit, and
compactions that lost the HEAD race. This change adds a simulated S3
backend to measure that, then cuts the request count and elects one
compactor per archive.

**Commit path.** Remote shards are uploaded straight to their final key
instead of staged and renamed. A commit starts from the manifest this
writer last published, so an uncontended flush reads nothing before its
compare-and-swap. A lost compare-and-swap re-reads HEAD, rebases, and
retries after a backoff from 0.5 s to 5 s for up to an hour of wall
time, so a flush does not fail under many writers. A one-row flush now
costs three requests instead of eight; a read view costs two instead of
three because a populated archive is validated from HEAD alone.

**Maintenance.** One writer per archive compacts at a time. The
maintenance pass takes a lease at `_maintenance` under the root and
publishes a manifest with the next `maintainer_epoch`; compaction
commits carry the epoch they were prepared under and are rejected once a
later maintainer announces itself. The lease is refreshed on a heartbeat
while compactions run. Writers without the lease flush and leave
compaction to the holder. The close-time merge is best effort: a closing
writer that holds the lease, or can take a free or stale one, merges
every writer's level-zero shards within the close budget, and a closer
that finds another writer maintaining the archive leaves its shards to
that writer. A wave of closing writers therefore elects one merger
instead of racing replacement commits. A writer from an older FineStore
build compacts without the lease and carries the epoch forward
unchanged.

**Lookups.** Each shard records its smallest and largest primary key
when keys are strings and integers. Lookups with `==` on a key prefix,
or `in` on the first key column, skip shards whose bounds exclude the
value, including blob descriptor reads. Shard schemas are cached per
process, and manifest shards are opened without the existence check
Arrow's fsspec handler issues first.

**Simulator.** `finestore.testing.simulated_s3` is an in-memory `s3://`
filesystem that charges one round trip per request, serves ranged reads
one block at a time, implements rename as COPY plus DELETE, and fails
overlapping conditional writes the way S3 does. It records every
request, so tests pin request budgets and
`lib/finestore/scripts/benchmark_multi_writer.py` compares commit
strategies without a bucket. The FineStore suite runs 64 behaviour tests
on both a local root and the simulated backend. The benchmark also takes
`--root` to drive the same writers against real storage.

Commit, conflict, compaction, abandonment, and lease counters are
exported as `finestore_*` telemetry.

**Simulator benchmark**, 100 ms per request at time scale 0.1 (elapsed
is raw at that scale; CPU work is not compressed), 8 flushes of 64 rows
per writer:

| writers, layout | elapsed s before → after | requests | compactions
(abandoned) | final shards | point lookup requests |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 16, shared root | 21.9 → 10.7 | 6737 → 1811 | 49 (30) → 2 (0) | 7 → 2
| 32 → 4 |
| 16, shared root, no maintenance | 12.2 → 7.6 | 2384 → 1947 | 16 (0) →
16 (0) | 16 → 16 | 68 → 5 |
| 16, per-writer roots | 4.9 → 3.2 | 1872 → 1246 | 16 (0) → 16 (0) | 16
→ 16 | 8 → 5 |
| 64, shared root, 4 flushes, scale 0.05 | 82.8 → 14.6 | 23331 → 8504 |
198 (130) → 2 (0) | 10 → 2 | 44 → 4 |

Before the backoff change, a 50 ms initial retry drove 64 writers to
about 29 conflicts per commit and 33k requests; the 0.5 s start cut that
to 11k with no loss in elapsed time, and electing one closer to merge
cut it to 8.5k with no abandoned compactions.

**GCS from an Iris job in the bucket's region** (`--root temp`, 8
flushes of 64 rows per writer; request counts are not observable there):

| writers, layout | elapsed s before → after | compactions (abandoned) |
final shards | point lookup s |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1, shared root | 9.6 → 5.7 | 1 (0) → 1 (0) | 1 → 1 | 0.30 → 0.18 |
| 4, shared root | 25.8 → 23.7 | 5 (1) → 4 (0) | 5 → 4 | 0.82 → 0.18 |
| 16, shared root | 162.3 → 76.3 | 41 (23) → 2 (0) | 6 → 2 | 1.07 → 0.18
|
| 16, shared root, no maintenance | 93.8 → 72.5 | 16 (0) → 16 (2) | 16 →
30 | 2.11 → 0.24 |
| 16, per-writer roots | 10.1 → 7.8 | 16 (0) → 16 (0) | 16 → 16 | 0.26 →
0.18 |
| 64, shared root, 4 flushes | 473.8 → 141.5 | 125 (81) → 3 (1) | 5 → 2
| 1.50 → 0.17 |

A shared root still commits at a fixed rate of roughly 1.5 flushes per
second, so each writer's flush latency grows linearly with the number of
writers; per-writer roots scale out. That serialization is inherent to
one compare-and-swapped HEAD and is what the proposal's per-writer logs
address. The 16- and 64-writer rows are from the elected close merge;
the other rows predate it. On GCS the 64 writers saw 1078 commit retries
and the 16 writers 168, counted from the retry log.

These measurements back the FineStore concurrency proposal in Loom
session bth4qn4d (artifact `finestore-improvements`): this is its P1;
per-writer logs and the key side table remain proposed.

commits.author: rjpower
commits.message:
Update holistic reviews in place and scale their walkthroughs (#10211)

Holistic re-reviews replace the original overview comment by its exact
ID and preserve finding numbers, including after a rebase. New or
materially changed actionable findings may also appear in one new
top-level PR comment linking to the overview. Separate markers keep that
comment out of overview discovery. If editing the overview fails, report
the failure without creating a duplicate. This prevents the repeated
walkthroughs seen on #10209.

Provide short and full review examples, a Mermaid flowchart example, and
explicit create-versus-edit instructions. Self-contained changes use
brief prose; larger changes can retain the system, motivation,
before/after, design, and limits outline. Use bold labels for short
sections and headings where they help navigation, and keep evidence with
the finding it supports.

commits.author: rjpower
commits.message:
Publish a stable Atlas catalog with FineStore range caching (#10208)

Publish production FULL campaigns directly to
`s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/rl-data/catalog/production` with an
explicit `--publish-catalog` option. Keep reports and artifacts
versioned, and keep local and SAMPLE catalogs separate. Seed the stable
catalog with the existing 206 source declarations, 146 assessments and
12,107 judgments with evidence packets. Retain its immutable shards in
the verified archive at
`s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/rl-data/migrations/2026-10-15/`.

Accumulate selected sources while preserving unselected entries and
their pinned dataset and pipeline declarations, including IDs absent
from an older checkout. Ignore superseded attempts per source using
retained campaign start times. Assessment keys include dataset
revisions, pipeline dependencies, rubric and model identity: a failed
changed-key assessment clears the old grade, while an exact-key retry
can reuse completed evidence. Check publication-lease ownership and the
starting catalog pointer before selecting a catalog snapshot.

Default Atlas imports to the stable root. Keep Postgres refresh explicit
and retryable, with a conditional serving-pointer update. Cleanup
deletes rows for load IDs observed before staging and always excludes
the currently served load. Reject imports whose source catalog changed
while loading. Grading, curriculum publication and Marina deployments
remain separate operations.

Replace FineStore's whole-shard cache admission with an LRU of requested
Parquet byte ranges. Each `ReadView` owns a configurable 64 MiB budget
shared across tables. Table and shard sizes do not determine admission;
reads larger than the budget bypass it. Fetch misses with ranged reads,
charge GCS transfer budgets for the requested bytes, and reject short
reads before caching. Blob decoding and Atlas evidence reads retain
their batch limits.

On the GCP assessment table's 19 shards, a 3.40-second cold scan warmed
the view's cache; all 146 subsequent source point lookups took 4.31
seconds in total. Without reader caching, three individual source
lookups on the same table took 7.03, 7.10 and 14.19 seconds.

Builds on #10207. The [Atlas incident
record](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/734) tracks catalog selection,
bootstrap and the production import.

commits.author: mcwitt
commits.message:
[levanter] Balance causal attention work across context shards in FA4 (#10170)

Hero training will switch to 262K context, which needs context
parallelism of at least CP4. Splitting the sequence contiguously across
the context shards ignores causality. The shard with the end of a long
document does far more attention work than the shard with its start. The
other ranks wait for that shard. This PR splits the queries in a zigzag
pattern inside the sharded FA4 wrapper, so every shard does about the
same attention work. On one GB200 NVL72 rack at 262K context (CP4/EP16,
restored from hero step 240000), tokens/s rise by 27.8%. Step time falls
from 29.66 s to 23.22 s, and its standard deviation falls from 3.19 s to
1.39 s.

For N context shards, the wrapper cuts the sequence into 2N chunks, and
shard c holds chunks 2c and 2c+1. Shard c swaps chunk 2c+1 with the
mirror shard N-1-c for chunk 2N-1-2c, so it attends one early chunk and
one matching late chunk. Then the outputs swap back.

The rest of the model keeps the sequence in order, so the embeddings,
RoPE, the short convolution, the labels, and the logits do not change.
The cost is two transfers of half of each shard's queries per layer,
plus their gradients in the backward pass. An earlier version of this PR
stored the whole sequence in zigzag order. That avoided the transfers
but touched every position-dependent op, with +477 lines in 10 files
instead of +109 in 2. On the same rack, that version measured 23.18 s
per step, so the transfers cost at most 0.2%. Every context-parallel FA4
caller, including snowball, now gets the balancing.

Both arms ran on the same rack, with 66 scored steps each. Peak memory
rose by 0.8 GiB, and the drop fraction stayed at 1.63%. Over 80 steps,
the loss differed from main by 4.6e-4 rms. The swap balances the work
within each row but not between rows. Balance between rows needs more
than one row per context group.

commits.author: rjpower
commits.message:
Cache small FineStore tables within each snapshot view (#10207)

Reuse immutable Parquet shard bytes across reads of small tables in
`ReadView`. The Atlas grading import made 438 keyed scans across three
GCP metadata tables totaling 6.8 MB. Each scan reopened the same shards;
individual assessment lookups took 7–14 seconds.

Tables other than blob tables can use an automatic cache when their
active shards total at most 8 MiB. Each view has a configurable 64 MiB
budget and reserves a table's full stored size before concurrent readers
fetch its shards. The cache holds compressed bytes; projection,
deduplication, filtering, and streaming stay in the existing reader.
Larger tables and blob tables retain their existing read paths. Cache
lifetime follows the pinned snapshot, so a new view observes later
commits.

With the shared cache, 146 standard assessment lookups over the same 19
shards completed in 8.17 seconds after a 3.14-second cold read. Atlas
uses its existing catalog and loader APIs without a client cache.

The related Atlas data incident is recorded in
[Echo](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/734).

commits.author: rjpower
commits.message:
Bound FineStore compaction with Arrow buffers (#10188)

Bound FineStore compaction to one decoded Parquet row group per input
shard. Each shard reader advances one group at a time with Parquet
pre-buffering disabled and a 1 MiB fsspec file cache. A decoded group or
required column read may exceed that byte cache.

Compaction takes the next available group by its first primary key. It
copies at most one row per key into an Arrow accumulator, replacing that
row only when a newer version appears. The accumulator has an explicit
400 MiB default byte target, configurable through
`DataStore(compaction_target_bytes=...)` or
`compact_table(target_bytes=...)`. Before adding a group that would
exceed the target, it concatenates and sorts the retained rows by
primary key, then writes one output shard. The shard writer splits that
output into Parquet row groups using its own row and byte limits. A
single large input group can exceed the compaction target, and
concatenation, sorting, and writing need additional memory. Group order
is approximate when an input shard is unsorted.

Keys may recur across output shards because the buffer can flush between
versions. FineStore readers select the newest version across shards, and
compaction cannot increase the total number of copies of a key. The
buffer targets one output shard but may write several; high compression
may produce more shards than the input.

This addresses memory exhaustion during checkpoint maintenance and close
reported by the [evaluation
workload](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/pull/212). Before
this change, a four-shard probe with 4 MiB document rows grew from 600
to 1,116 MiB of Arrow allocations as input rose from 32 to 64 rows per
shard. An earlier bounded-scan probe stayed near 140–144 MiB. The
current regression sets a 4 MiB compaction target, doubles input rows,
and checks bounded Arrow allocation growth and newest-value selection.
All 114 FineStore tests pass.

commits.author: yonromai
commits.message:
[iris] Resolve personal identities at controller startup (#10070)

Resolve opaque principal references in roles, budgets, and federation admission from a private directory when the controller starts. Exact account roles override the admin list and provider default in both Python and Rust.

The marin Pulumi stack derives the ID-to-email directory from the encrypted IAM registry and publishes it as a Secret Manager secret. The payload is marked secret, so previews hide its contents and the stack’s KMS secrets provider encrypts its copy in state. GCP controllers load it at runtime; CoreWeave deployment passes it through the controller-only `iris-controller-env` Kubernetes Secret. ConfigMaps and VM bootstrap configs retain opaque principal IDs and secret references.

Deployment validates the directory before stopping a controller. Startup resolves identities before checkpoint or database changes. Merge this support before #9846 and #10063, and publish the reviewed directory and read grants before rolling out their configs.

[iris] Grant federation access to the GB200 cluster (#10186)

Admit an additional researcher through `auth.allowed_submitters` on
`cw-us-east-08a`. IAP login and hub status checks already work, but the
GB200 peer rejects job handoffs because the submitting identity is
absent from its allowlist.

The allowlist is loaded at controller startup, so activate the grant
with a `cw-us-east-08a` controller rollout after merge. Internal
onboarding now explains the separate peer admission check. This
completes the GB200 access intended by #10182 and follows the existing
H100 grant in #10056.

[iac] Grant Iris cluster access to a new researcher (#10182)

Grant an encrypted human principal `roles/iap.httpsResourceAccessor` on
`iris-marin-be` and `iris-marin-dev-be` for research on the GB200 NVL72
cluster, `cw-us-east-08a`. The production `marin` gateway federates jobs
to that cluster and its other configured peers. Its
`auth.iap.unprovisioned_role: admin` setting gives users admitted
through IAP shared Iris admin access.

A separate reviewer should run `review-grant`, confirm the decrypted
principal and scope, merge, and apply the `marin` stack in
`infra/pulumi`. This grants no project-wide GCP IAM roles or direct
CoreWeave Kubernetes access.
